Silting reduction and picture categories of 0-Auslander extriangulated categories Thanks: The author acknowledges support from the French ANR grant CHARMS (ANR-19-CE40-0017-02).
Erlend D. Børve

Abstract
. Let 𝒞 \mathcal{C} be an extriangulated category and let ℛ ⊆ 𝒞 \mathcal{R}\subseteq\mathcal{C} be a rigid subcategory. Generalizing Iyama–Yang silting reduction, we devise a technical condition (gCP) on ℛ \mathcal{R} which is sufficient for the Verdier quotient 𝒞 / thick ⁡ ( ℛ ) \mathcal{C}/\mathrm{thick}(\mathcal{R}) to be equivalent to an ideal quotient. In particular, the Verdier quotient 𝒞 / thick ⁡ ( ℛ ) \mathcal{C}/\mathrm{thick}(\mathcal{R}) will admit an extriangulation in such a way that the localization functor L ℛ : 𝒞 → 𝒞 / thick ⁡ ( ℛ ) L_{\mathcal{R}}\colon\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}/\mathrm{thick}(\mathcal{R}) is extriangulated. When 𝒞 \mathcal{C} is 0-Auslander, the condition (gCP) holds for all rigid subcategories ℛ \mathcal{R} admitting Bongartz completions. Furthermore, we prove that the Verdier quotient 𝒞 / thick ⁡ ( ℛ ) \mathcal{C}/\mathrm{thick}(\mathcal{R}) then remains 0-Auslander. As an application, we define the picture category of a 0 0 -Auslander exact dg category 𝒜 \mathscr{A} with Bongartz completions, which generalizes the notion of τ \tau -cluster morphism category. We show that the picture category of 𝒜 \mathscr{A} is a cubical category, in the sense of Igusa. The picture group of 𝒜 \mathscr{A} is defined as the fundamental group of its picture category. When H 0 ​ 𝒜 H_{0}\mathscr{A} is 𝐠 \mathbf{g} -finite, the picture group of 𝒜 \mathscr{A} is finitely presented.



2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
16B50, 16E45, 18G35, 18G80

0.
Introduction

0.1.

Additive categorifications of cluster algebras
[
BMR+06
,
Ami09
]
have had a revolutionary impact on the representation theory of associative algebras. In classical tilting theory
[
BB06
,
HR82
]
, the mutation of a tilting module at an indecomposable direct summand is not always defined, but by modelling this mutation procedure on the mutation of seeds in cluster algebras, one obtains mutationally complete generalizations of tilting theory. Notable frameworks include cluster tilting theory
[
BMR07
]
,
\tau
-tilting theory
[
AIR14
]
and two-term silting
[
IJY14
]
. There is also a rich interaction with torsion theories, t-strucutres, co-t-strucutres, as well as other category-theoretic notions
[
KY14
,
BY14
]
.

0.2.

The mutational completeness of support
\tau
-tilting pairs and two-term silting complexes gives rise to reduction techniques, known as
\tau
-tilting reduction
[
Jas15
,
BM21
]
and silting reduction
[
IY18
,
IY20
]
, respectively.
One can think of the
\tau
-cluster morphism category as a categorification these reduction techniques.
The first definitions
\tau
-cluster morphism categories were confined to hereditary algebras of type
A
, where the definition is combinatorial in nature
[
Igu14
,
CN17
]
. Later, the definition took a representation-theoretic form, extending the setting to representation-finite herediary algebras
[
IT17
]
, then to
\tau
-tilting finite algebras
[
BM21
]
, and ultimately to all finite-dimensional algebras
[
BH23
]
. When going beyond the hereditary case, the composition rule was defined in terms of support
\tau
-tilting reduction
[
BM21
, §3]
, a class of bijections defined in a case-by-case manner. When composing maps, the number of cases multiplies, rendering the proof of the associative property rather involved
[
BM21
, §§5–10]
.

0.3.

There are two generalized approaches to
\tau
-cluster morphism categories that considerably simplify the proof of the associative property. In previous work, the author defined the
\tau
-cluster morphism category of a connective differential graded algebra with finite-dimensional homology in all degrees
[
Bør21
]
. In this homological approach, one defines the composition rule using Iyama–Yang silting reduction
[
IY18
,
IY20
]
, whose functoriality leads to a short proof of associativity. The second framework is combinatorial, and is due to Schroll–Tattar–Treffinger–Williams
[
STTW23
]
and Kaipel
[
Kai23
]
. The former set of authors show that the
\tau
-cluster morphism category can be recovered from the wall-and-chamber structure, whereas Kaipel generalizes their work by developing the of notion partitioned fan and then extracting a category from the underlying geometry.

0.4.
Summary of results

In
Section

1
, we give a brief introduction to the theory of exact dg categories, following Chen
[
Che24
,
Che23
]
. Very roughly speaking, one arrives at the definition by accommodating Keller’s minimal axioms
[
Kel90
, Appendix A]
of Quillen exact categories
[
Qui73
]
in the framework of differential graded categories. We recall in
Section

2.8
how the zeroth homology category of an exact dg category admits the structure of an extriangulated category, in the sense of Nakaoka–Palu
[
NP19
]
.
We give a brief overview of localization theory for extriangulated categories in
Section

3
. In
Section

4
, we recall the notions of rigid and silting subcategories of an extriangulated category, with emphasis on the case of 0-Auslander extriangulated categories, in the sense of Gorsky–Nakaoka–Palu
[
GNP23
]
.

Our original contributions are in
Sections

5
and
6
. In
Section

5
, we generalize Iyama–Yang silting reduction
[
IY18
,
IY20
]
to extriangulated categories, extending the scope provided by the current literature
[
LZZZ21
,
PZ24
,
LZ24
]
. The following technical condition will be imposed in
Section

5.7
.

Condition
(gCP)

Let
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
be an extriangulated category. Consider the following condition on a rigid subcategory
\mathcal{R}
of
\mathcal{C}
:

The ordered tuple
\big((\mathcal{R}^{\vee},\mathcal{R}^{\perp}),({{}^{\perp}\mathcal{R}},\mathcal{R}^{\wedge})\big)
is a generalized concentric twin cotorsion pair (henceforth shortened to gCTCP) in
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
, where we use the notation introduced in
5.1.
Setup

5.1
.

Our main results will be the following.

Theorem
5.9
.

Let
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
be a 0-Auslander extriangulated category and let
\mathcal{R}\subseteq\mathcal{C}
be a rigid subcategory.
Then
\mathcal{R}
admits Bongartz completions (see
Section

4.12
) precisely when
\big((\mathcal{R},\mathcal{R}^{\perp}),({{}^{\perp}\mathcal{R}},\mathcal{R})\big)
is a gCTCP in
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
. In particular,
Condition
(gCP)
holds for all rigid subcategories of
\mathcal{C}
admitting Bongartz completions.

Theorem
5.13
.

Let
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
be an extriangulated category and let
\mathcal{R}\subseteq\mathcal{C}
be a rigid subcategory.

We spend

of a 0-Auslander exact dg category
\mathscr{A}
(with cofibrant mapping complexes) in which all rigid subcategories of the extriangulated category

admit Bongartz completions. By considering the special case

, and the

is the fundamental group of the picture space. If the extriangulated category

is Krull–Schmidt and contains a silting object. then the picture category

6.8

6.11

is finitely presented if
\mathscr{A}
is
\mathbf{g}
-finite.

0.5.
Notation and conventions

A Grothendieck universe
\mathfrak{U}
is fixed throughout, and
\mathfrak{U}
-small sets will simply be called
small
. We say that a category
\mathcal{C}
is
small
the set
\bigsqcup_{x,y\in\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{C}(x,y)
is small. All sets and categories we fix in our results are small, unless declared as
large
.
A small field
\mathit{k}
is fixed throughout.

We employ the homological indexing convention for complexes.
Let
\Mod(\mathit{k})
denote the monoidal category of
\mathit{k}
-modules, and
\Ch(\mathit{k})
that of chain complexes thereof.
A
k
-category
is an enriched category over
\Mod(\mathit{k})
, whereas a
dg
k
-category
is enriched over
\Ch(\mathit{k})
. The differential in a dg category will be denoted
\partial
.
By considering the underlying
\mathit{k}
-categories, one defines a notion of smallness for (dg)
\mathit{k}
-categories.

Given a dg
\mathit{k}
-category
\mathscr{A}
, one can produce two
\mathit{k}
-categories, denoted
Z_{0}\mathscr{A}
and
H_{0}\mathscr{A}
, having the same objects as
\mathscr{A}

\mathit{k}
-category
H_{0}\mathscr{A}
will be called the
zeroth homology
\mathit{k}
-category
of
\mathscr{A}
. We have that
H_{0}\mathscr{A}
is small precisely when
\mathscr{A}
is small.
Since a dg subcategory of a dg
\mathit{k}
-category
\mathscr{A}
is uniquely determined by the induced subcategory of
H_{0}\mathscr{A}
, we will often implicitly descend to
H_{0}\mathscr{A}
when defining dg subcategories of
\mathscr{A}
.

The category of small dg
\mathit{k}
-categories admits a cofibrantly generated model structure in which the weak equivalences are the quasi-equivalences
[
Tab05
]
. This model category will be denoted
\dgcat_{\mathit{k}}
, and its homotopy category will be denoted
\Hqe_{\mathit{k}}
.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}}

[
BK90
]
. Since morphisms in a pretriangulated dg
\mathit{k}
-category admit a homotopy kernel and a homotopy cokernel, and the class of conflations that arise in this way define an exact structure on
\mathscr{A}

[
Che24

. Pretriangulated dg
\mathit{k}

\mathit{k}

1.9.

The bounded derived dg
\mathit{k}
-category of a small connective exact dg
\mathit{k}
-category is small by construction. For an arbitrary additive dg
\mathit{k}
-category
\mathfrak{a}
, we will also need to consider the
derived
\mathit{k}
-category

\mathscr{D}(\mathfrak{a})
of
\mathfrak{a}
, which is defined as the localization of
\mathscr{C}(\mathfrak{a})
with respect to the
quasi-isomorphisms
, namely the class of morphisms in
\mathscr{C}(\mathfrak{a})
inducing quasi-isomorphisms of complexes when evaluated at any object in
\mathfrak{a}
. The derived
\mathit{k}
-category of
\mathfrak{a}
is pretriangulated, but not hardly ever small.

1.10.
Example

(i)

[
Che24
, Example 4.6]
Any
\mathit{k}
-category can be regarded as a dg
\mathit{k}
-category in which all mapping complexes are stalk complexes.
Specializing the axioms of exact dg
\mathit{k}
-categories to
\mathit{k}
-categories recovers the notion of Quillen exact
\mathit{k}
-categories
[
Qui73
]

[
Kel90
, Appendix A]
. Consequently, any Quillen exact
\mathit{k}
-category can be regarded as an exact dg
\mathit{k}
-category. In particular, any abelian
\mathit{k}
-category is naturally equipped with an exact structure, if regarded as a dg
\mathit{k}
-category.

(ii)

Inside the derived dg
\mathit{k}
-category
\mathscr{D}(\mathfrak{a})
of an additive dg
\mathit{k}
-category
\mathfrak{a}
sits the smallest pretriangulated subcategory closed under direct summands containing
\mathfrak{a}
. This is denoted
\per(\mathfrak{a})
, and called the
perfect derived dg
\mathit{k}
-category
of
\mathfrak{a}
. We note that although
\mathscr{D}(\mathfrak{a})
is not small, the dg subcategory
\per(\mathfrak{a})
is. Inside
\per(\mathfrak{a})
sits the
two-term dg
\mathit{k}
-category of
\mathfrak{a}
, namely the full subcategory spanned by the objects
x
that appear in a conflation of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sigma a_{1}}

where
a_{0}
and
a_{1}
are in the essential image of the embedding
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{a}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\per(\mathfrak{a})}
. One sees that this defines an extension-closed dg subcategory of
\per(\mathfrak{a})
, whence it admits the structure of exact dg
\mathit{k}
-category by
Section

1.7
.
Throughout this text, the two-term dg
\mathit{k}
-category of
\mathfrak{a}
will be denoted
\per_{[0,1]}(\mathfrak{a})
. When
\mathfrak{a}
consists of a single object whose endomorphism dg
\mathit{k}
-algebra is
A
, we write
\per_{[0,1]}(A)
instead of
\per_{[0,1]}(\mathfrak{a})
. The
two-term category
of
\mathfrak{a}
is defined as
H_{0}\per_{[0,1]}(\mathfrak{a})
.

2.
Extriangulated categories

2.1.

In order to recall the definition of an extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category, some preparation of terminology will be needed. Although the original axioms are due to Nakaoka–Palu
[
NP19
, Definition 2.12]
, we will present the axioms of 1-exangulated
\mathit{k}
-categories, an equivalent notion put forward by Herschend–Liu–Nakaoka
[
HLN21
, Definition 2.32 and Proposition 4.3]
.

, i.e. the first morphism is natural when
a\oplus c
is regarded as a coproduct of
a
and
c
, and the latter is natural when
a\oplus c
is regarded as a product.

(ii)

For
\xi\in\mathbb{E}(c,a)
and
\xi^{\prime}\in\mathbb{E}(c^{\prime},a^{\prime})
, we have that
\mathfrak{s}(\xi\oplus\xi^{\prime})=\mathfrak{s}(\xi)\oplus\mathfrak{s}(\xi^{\prime})
in
\mathbb{E}(c\oplus c^{\prime},a\oplus a^{\prime})
.

A definition along these lines has been put forward in previous work of the author with P. Trygsland
[
BT21
, Definition 4.4]
.
Consider the subcategory
\mathcal{H}^{y}_{3\mathrm{t}}(\mathcal{C})
of
\mathcal{H}_{3\mathrm{t}}(\mathcal{C})
containing all objects, but containing only the morphisms of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\iota}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\iota^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi^{\prime}}

where the outer morphisms are identity morphisms in
\mathcal{C}
.
For each pair of objects
a,c\in\mathcal{C}
, the functor
\mathfrak{s}
induces a map from
\mathbb{E}(c,a)
to the set of isomorphism classes in
\mathcal{H}^{y}_{3\mathrm{t}}(\mathcal{C})
of conflations of the form

(2.2.c)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c.}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\iota}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi}

Our functorial definition of exact realizations is thus consistent with the definitions elsewhere in the literature
[
NP19
, §2.2]

[
HLN21
, §2.4]
.

Given an exact realization
\mathfrak{s}
of
\mathbb{E}
, consider the three-term complex in (
2.2.c
) as an object in
\mathcal{H}_{3\mathrm{t}}(\mathcal{C})
.
The three-term complexes in the image of
\mathfrak{s}
will be called
\mathfrak{s}
-conflations
, or just
conflations
when
\mathfrak{s}
can be safely suppressed from the notation. A
morphism of (
\mathfrak{s}
-)conflations
is simply a morphism of the underlying complexes. The morphism
\iota
in (
2.2.c
) is called an
(
\mathfrak{s}
-)inflation
, whereas
\pi
is a(n
\mathfrak{s}
-)deflation
. In our diagrams, we will decorate inflations and deflations as we have in (
2.2.c
).

2.3.
Definition

[
HLN21
, Definition 2.32]
. Let
\mathcal{C}
be an additive
\mathit{k}
-category, let

be an additive bifunctor, and let
\mathfrak{s}
be an exact realization of
\mathbb{E}
. Then the triple
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E},\mathfrak{s})
is called an
extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category
if the following axioms hold:

(Extr1)

Composites of
\mathfrak{s}
-deflations are
\mathfrak{s}
-deflations, and composites of
\mathfrak{s}
-inflations are
\mathfrak{s}
-inflations.

(Extr2)

\mathfrak{s}
-deflations admit
good lifts
in the following precise sense: given the solid part of the diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\iota^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 1_{a}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\iota}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi}

where the bottom row is an
\mathfrak{s}
-conflation, we can add the dashed arrows to produce a morphism of
\mathfrak{s}
-conflations in which the leftmost vertical morphism is an identity morphism. Moreover, we require the “folded” complex

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b\oplus c^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{pmatrix}f^{\prime}\\
\pi^{\prime}\end{pmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{pmatrix}-\pi&f\end{pmatrix}}

to be an
\mathfrak{s}
-conflation.

(Extr2
op
)

\mathfrak{s}
-inflations admit good lifts, in the dual sense of
(Extr2)
.

If
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E},\mathfrak{s})
is an extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category, we say that that
\mathbb{E}
and
\mathfrak{s}
form an
extriangulation
on the underlying additive
\mathit{k}
-category
\mathcal{C}
.
The extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E},\mathfrak{s})
will be denoted
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
, or simply
\mathcal{C}
, whenever reference to the exact realization and/or the bifunctor is unnecessary.

2.4.

Given a conflation

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\iota}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi}

in an extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category
\mathcal{C}
, we say that

(i)

c
is a
cone
of
\iota
,

(ii)

a
is a
cocone
of
\pi
,

(iii)

b
is an
extension
of
c
in
a
.

Analogously to
Section

1.7
, we say that a full subcategory
\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathcal{C}
is
extension-closed
if it is closed under the formation of extensions. We define the notions of
closure under cones
and
closure under cocones
similiarly.

Whenever it is unnecessary to explicitly mention the natural transformation giving
F
the structure of an extriangulated functor, we will refrain from doing so. We will often say that a
\mathit{k}
-linear functor
F

when there is an obvious choice of natural transformation
\psi
such that the pair
(F,\psi)
is an extriangulated functor.

2.6.

[
NP19
, Remark 2.18]

We have the following counterpart of
Section

1.7
:
Let
\mathcal{C}^{\prime}
be an extension-closed subcategory of an extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
.
The restriction
\mathbb{E}^{\prime}
of
\mathbb{E}
to
\mathcal{C}
determines an extriangulation on
\mathcal{C}^{\prime}
, and
(\mathcal{C}^{\prime},\mathbb{E}^{\prime})
is an extriangulated subcategory of
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
.

2.8.

Let
\mathscr{A}
be an exact dg
\mathit{k}
-category.
Then the
\mathit{k}
-category
H_{0}\mathscr{A}
can be equipped with an extriangulation
[
Che24
, Theorem 4.26]
. This generalizes Bondal–Kapranov’s result on the triangulation on the zeroth homology category of pretriangulated dg
\mathit{k}
-category
[
BK90
, Proposition 2]
. Whenever the exact structure
\mathcal{S}
is suppressed from the notation, we will denote the bifunctor in (
2.8.a
) below by
\mathbb{E}_{\mathscr{A}}
. In the same spirit, we denote the associated extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category by the pair by
(H_{0}\mathscr{A},\mathbb{E}_{\mathscr{A}})
, or simply by
H_{0}\mathscr{A}
. An extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category is called
algebraic
if there exists a
\mathit{k}
-linear extriangulated equivalence to an extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category of the form
(H_{0}\mathscr{A},\mathbb{E}_{\mathscr{A}})
for some exact dg
\mathit{k}
-category
\mathscr{A}
.
If an extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
is equivalent to
(H_{0}\mathscr{A},\mathbb{E}_{\mathscr{A}})
, we will say that
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
is
enhanced
by
\mathscr{A}
, or that
\mathscr{A}
is a(n
exact) dg enhancement
of
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
.

We briefly recall how the extriangulation on
H_{0}\mathscr{A}
comes about. Chen constructs the bifunctor

(2.9.a)

Since
\mathscr{D}_{\mathrm{dg}}^{\mathrm{b}}(\tau_{\geq 0}\mathscr{A})
is a pretriangulated dg
\mathit{k}
-category, we have that

is an algebraic triangulated
\mathit{k}
-category
[
Kel99
, 2.1, 2.2]
. It follows that any extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category admitting a dg enhancement can be obtained as an extension-closed subcategory of an algebraic triangulated
\mathit{k}
-category.

3.
Localization

3.1.

[
GZ12
]
Let
\mathcal{C}
be a category and let
\mathcal{S}
be a set of morphisms in
\mathcal{C}
. A
Gabriel–Zisman localization
of
\mathcal{C}
with respect to

A Gabriel–Zisman localization always exists (up to set-theoretic issues), and is clearly unique up to natural isomorphism. In the cases where
\mathcal{C}
is closed under composition, one may also refer to
\mathcal{S}
as a subcategory of
\mathcal{C}
.

3.3.

Let
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
be an extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category. Alike the special case of triangulated
\mathit{k}
-categories
[
Ver96
, §2.1]
, one can use Gabriel–Zisman localization of develop a notion of localization.
A
thick subcategory
of
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
is a full subcategory
\mathcal{N}\subseteq\mathcal{C}
which is

(i)

closed under isomorphisms and direct summands,

(ii)

it is extension-closed, closed under cones, and closed under cocones.

The smallest thick subcategory of
\mathcal{C}
containing a full subcategory
\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathcal{C}
will be denoted
\thick_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{X})
, or simply
\thick(\mathcal{X})
when the ambient extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category
\mathcal{C}
is clear from context. For a thick subcategory
\mathcal{N}
of
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
let
\mathit{Inf}_{\mathcal{N}}
be the set of inflations in
\mathcal{C}
with cone in
\mathcal{N}
. Dually, we define
\mathit{Def}_{\mathcal{N}}
as the set of deflations in
\mathcal{C}
with cocone in
\mathcal{N}
. Defining the subcategory
\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{N}}
of
\mathcal{C}
as the smallest subcategory of
\mathcal{C}
containing both
\mathit{Inf}_{\mathcal{N}}
or
\mathit{Def}_{\mathcal{N}}
, one defines the
Verdier localization functor
of
\mathcal{C}
with respect to
\mathcal{N}
as the Gabriel–Zisman localization of
\mathcal{C}
with respect to
\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{N}}
.

L_{\mathcal{N}}\colon(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})\mathchoice{\hskip 2.15277pt\hbox to17.62pt{\vbox to13.73pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 0.2pt\lower-3.42159pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1}

. The codomain
\mathcal{C}/\mathcal{N}
of this functor is called the
Verdier quotient
of
\mathcal{C}
with respect to
\mathcal{N}
. We say that the thick subcategory
\mathcal{N}

admits a calculus of left fractions
if the subcategory
\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{N}}
admits a calculus of left fractions, in the sense of Gabriel–Zisman
[
GZ12
, §I.2]
.
It is not true in general that the Verdier quotient
\mathcal{C}/\mathcal{N}
admits an extriangulation, even when
\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{N}}
admits a calculus of left fractions; the axiom
(Extr1)
need not hold unless
\mathcal{N}
is biresolving or percolating
[
NOS22
, §4]
.
However, since
\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{N}}
contains all isomorphisms and is closed under the composition and the formation of direct sums, the Verdier quotient
\mathcal{C}/\mathcal{N}
becomes weakly extriangulated, in the sense of Baillargeon–Brüstle–Gorsky–Hassoun
[
BBGH22
]
.

3.4.

Let
\mathscr{A}
be a dg
\mathit{k}
-category and let
\mathcal{S}
be a subcategory of
H_{0}\mathscr{A}
. For a dg
\mathit{k}
-category
\mathscr{B}
, let
\Hqe_{k}(\mathscr{A},\mathscr{B})_{\mathcal{S}}
denote the subset of
\Hqe_{\mathit{k}}(\mathscr{A},\mathscr{B})
consisting of the exact morphisms

) is zero. An
\mathbb{E}
-projective-injective object
in
\mathcal{C}
is both
\mathbb{E}
-projective and
\mathbb{E}
-injective. We will simply use the terms
projective
,
injective
and
projective-injective
when there can be no confusion as to the choice of bifunctor
\mathbb{E}
.
Let
\mathrm{proj}(\mathcal{C})
(resp.
\mathrm{inj}(\mathcal{C})
, resp.
\mathrm{proj\mathchar 45\relax inj}(\mathcal{C})
) denote the full subcategory of
\mathcal{C}
spanned by the projective (resp. injective, resp. projective-injective) objects in
\mathcal{C}
.
An extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})

has enough projectives
if one for every object
x\in\mathcal{C}
can find a deflation
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi}
, where
q
is projective. Such a deflation will be called a
projective cover
of
x
.
The notions of
having enough injectives
and
injective envelopes
are defined dually.

4.3.

In the same spririt as Yoneda’s construction for abelian
\mathit{k}
-categories
[

]
, one defines the higher extension functors

, Definition 3.1]
. The functor

, whereas

, both by definition.
If

as higher Ext-functors in the bounded derived dg
\mathit{k}
-category of

[

, Proposition 6.24]
.

Suppose that the extriangulated

-category

has enough projectives. For an object

. A dual result holds when

4.5.

[
GNP23
, Definition 3.7]

The extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
is
0-Auslander
if it has enough projecitives, is hereditary, and any projective object
p\in\mathcal{C}
is the domain of an inflation
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q}
with projective-injective codomain. A 0-Auslander extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
is
reduced
if every projective-injective object therein is a zero object.

An exact dg
\mathit{k}
-category
\mathscr{A}
is called
0-Auslander
if
(H_{0}\mathscr{A},\mathbb{E}_{\mathscr{A}})
is 0-Auslander as an extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category. A 0-Auslander exact dg
\mathit{k}
-category
\mathscr{A}
is
reduced
if
(H_{0}\mathscr{A},\mathbb{E}_{\mathscr{A}})
is reduced.

4.6.
Example

We include two classes of examples of 0-Auslander extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-categories.

(i)

[
GNP23
, §3.3.8]
Let
A
be a connective dg
\mathit{k}
-algebra. Regarding
A
as a dg
\mathit{k}
-category with one object, let
H_{0}\per_{[0,1]}(A)
be the two-term category of
A
, as defined in
1.10.
Example

1.10
(ii)
. This is an example of a reduced 0-Auslander exact dg
\mathit{k}
-category.

(ii)

[
GNP23
, §3.3.2]

For a positive integer
n
, let
\Lambda_{n}
be the path
\mathit{k}
-algebra of the linearly oriented
A_{n}
-quiver

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 1}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 2}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n.}

Then the abelian category
\fgMod(\Lambda_{n})
of finite-dimensional right
\Lambda_{n}
-modules is a 0-Auslander extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category.
Among these, only
\fgMod(\Lambda_{1})
is reduced; for

there is exactly one non-zero projective-injective object in
\fgMod(\Lambda_{n})
up to isomorphism.

4.7.

Let
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
be an extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category.
A full subcategory
\mathcal{R}\subseteq\mathcal{C}
is called
rigid (with respect to
\mathbb{E}
)
if it is closed under isomorphism and
\mathbb{E}^{i}(r,r^{\prime})=0
for all
i\geq 1
and
r,r^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}
.
A rigid subcategory
\mathcal{R}\subseteq\mathcal{C}
is
silting
if additionally
\thick(\mathcal{R})=\mathcal{C}
.
Let
\mathrm{rigid}(\mathcal{C})
denote the set of rigid subcategories of
\mathcal{C}
, and
\mathrm{silt}(\mathcal{C})
the set of silting subcategories of
\mathcal{C}
. Given a rigid subcategory
\mathcal{R}\subseteq\mathcal{C}
, let
\mathrm{rigid}_{\mathcal{R}}(\mathcal{C})
(resp.
\mathrm{silt}_{\mathcal{R}}(\mathcal{C})
) denote subset of
\mathrm{rigid}(\mathcal{C})
(resp.
\mathrm{silt}(\mathcal{C})
) consisting of the subcategories containing
\mathcal{R}
.
An object
t\in\mathcal{C}
is
rigid
(resp.
silting
) if the smallest additive subcategory of
\mathcal{C}
containing
t
, denoted
\add(t)
, is rigid (resp. silting).

Let
\mathscr{A}
be an exact dg
\mathit{k}
-category. A full dg subcategory
\mathscr{R}\subseteq\mathscr{A}
is called
rigid
(resp.
silting
) if
H_{0}\mathscr{R}
is a rigid (resp. silting) subcategory of
H_{0}\mathscr{A}
. The notions of a
rigid object
and
silting object
in
\mathscr{A}
are defined similarly.
In accordance with the notation introduced above, we define the sets
\mathrm{rigid}(\mathscr{A})
,
\mathrm{silt}(\mathscr{A})
, etc., in the same way.

4.9.

Let
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
be an extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category.
Then the set
\mathrm{silt}(\mathcal{C})
admits the structure of a poset, where we set
\mathcal{R}\geq\mathcal{R}^{\prime}
if
\mathbb{E}^{i}(r,r^{\prime})=0
for all
i\geq 1
,
r\in\mathcal{R}
and
r^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}^{\prime}

[
AT22
, Proposition 5.12]
. In particular, if
\mathcal{C}
is hereditary, we have that
\mathcal{R}\geq\mathcal{R}^{\prime}
precisely when
\mathbb{E}(r,r^{\prime})=0
for all
r\in\mathcal{R}
and
r^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}^{\prime}
.

4.10.

If an extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
is Krull-Schmidt and contains a silting object
t
, then all silting subcategories of
\mathcal{C}
are of the form
\add(s)
for some silting object
s\in\mathcal{C}

[
AT22
, Proposition 5.4]
, and every silting object has the same number of indecomposable direct summands up to isomorphism
[
AT23
, Theorem 4.1]
.

Suppose that the extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
is 0-Auslander. Then a rigid subcategory of
\mathcal{C}
is silting precisely when it is maximal with respect to the rigidity property
[
GNP23
, Theorem 4.3]
.
Using the definition of projective and injective objects in
Section

4.1
, it is easy to see that both
\mathrm{proj}(\mathcal{C})
and
\mathrm{inj}(\mathcal{C})
form maximally rigid subcategories of
\mathcal{C}
. It is also easy to see that
\mathrm{proj}(\mathcal{C})
is the maximal element in the poset
\mathrm{silt}(\mathcal{C})
. Dually, we have that
\mathrm{inj}(\mathcal{C})
is the minimal element. When
\mathcal{C}
is algebraic and enhanced by an exact dg
k
-category
\mathscr{A}
, we will denote the maximal and minimal elements in
\mathrm{silt}(\mathscr{A})
by
\mathscr{P}_{\mathscr{A}}
and
\mathscr{I}_{\mathscr{A}}
, respectively.

4.12.

Any rigid subcategory
\mathcal{R}
of a 0-Auslander extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
is a subcategory of a silting subcategory of
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
. One defines the
maximal Bongartz completion

\mathcal{R}_{+}
as the smallest additive subcategory of
\mathcal{C}
containing
\mathcal{R}
, the projective-injective objects in
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
, as well as all objects of the form
u_{r}^{y}
appearing in a conflation

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u_{r}^{y}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{y}}

in which
y\in\mathrm{inj}(\mathcal{C})
and
p_{y}
is a right
\add(\mathcal{R},\mathrm{proj}(\mathcal{C})\cap\mathrm{inj}(\mathcal{C}))
-approximation. We say that
\mathcal{R}

admits a maximal Bongartz completion
if the deflation and right approximation
p_{y}
exists for all injective objects
y\in\mathcal{C}
.
This is indeed a silting subcategory of
\mathcal{C}
containing
\mathcal{R}

[
GNP23
, Corollary 4.8]
, and it is the maximal such silting subcategory with respect to the partial order in
Section

4.9
(this is shown using a long-exact sequence argument, see (
4.4.a
), and heredity). One defines the
minimal Bongartz completion

\mathcal{R}_{\div}
dually, and this is the minimal silting subcategory of
\mathcal{C}
containing
\mathcal{R}
. We say that
\mathcal{R}

admits Bongartz completions
if it admits a maximal and a minimal Bongartz completion.

5.
Silting reduction for extriangulated categories

5.1.
Setup

We fix an extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
.
For a full subcategory
\mathcal{X}
of
\mathcal{C}
, let
\mathcal{X}^{\perp}
(resp.
{{}^{\perp}\mathcal{X}}
) denote the full subcategory of
\mathcal{C}
spanned by the objects
y\in\mathcal{C}
with the property that
\mathbb{E}^{i}(x,y)=0
(resp.
\mathbb{E}^{i}(y,x)=0
) for all
x\in\mathcal{X}
and all positive integers
i
. We write
\mathcal{X}^{\perp_{\mathcal{C}}}
(resp.
{{}^{\perp_{\mathcal{C}}}\mathcal{X}}
) when the choice of ambient extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category may be unclear. Let
\mathcal{X}^{\vee}
(resp.
\mathcal{X}^{\wedge}
) denote the smallest full subcategory of
\mathcal{C}
containing
\mathcal{X}
which is closed under extensions, cocones (resp. cones) and direct summands.

Given a rigid subcategory
\mathcal{R}\subseteq\mathcal{C}
, let
\mathcal{Z}_{\mathcal{R}}
denote the full subcategory
{\mathcal{R}^{\perp}\cap{{}^{\perp}\mathcal{R}}}\subseteq\mathcal{C}
. One uses long-exact sequence arguments (
Section

4.4
) to show that
\mathcal{Z}_{\mathcal{R}}
is extension-closed in
\mathcal{C}
, which lets us induce an extriangulation on
\mathcal{Z}_{\mathcal{R}}
using
Section

2.6
.
The
reduced category
of
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
with respect to
\mathcal{R}
is given by ideal quotient

\overline{\mathcal{C}}_{\mathcal{R}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{\mbox{\scriptsize{def}}}}}{{\,=\,}}\mathcal{Z}_{\mathcal{R}}/[\mathcal{R}].

Since all objects in
\mathcal{R}
are projective-injective in
\mathcal{Z}_{\mathcal{R}}
, the restriction of
\mathbb{E}
to
\mathcal{Z}_{\mathcal{R}}
induces a
\mathit{k}
-linear bifunctor
\overline{\mathbb{E}}
on
\overline{\mathcal{C}}_{\mathcal{R}}
, yielding an extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category
(\overline{\mathcal{C}}_{\mathcal{R}},\overline{\mathbb{E}})
. By
Section

3.2
, the ideal quotient functor

5.2.
Proposition

Let
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
be an extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category with enough projectives or injectives, and let
\mathcal{R}\subseteq\mathcal{C}
be a rigid subcategory.

(i)

For any
i\geq 0
, the bifunctors
\overline{\mathbb{E}^{i}}
and
\overline{\mathbb{E}}^{i}
are naturally isomorphic.

(ii)

For all
x\in{{}^{\perp}\mathcal{R}}
,
y\in\mathcal{R}^{\perp}
, and
i>0
, the
\mathit{k}
-vector space
\mathbb{E}^{i}(x,y)
is trivial precisely when
\overline{\mathbb{E}}^{i}(x,y)
is trivial.

Proof.

We prove
(i)
in the case where
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
has enough projectives, noting that the case of enough injectives is dual.
We proceed by induction on
i
. The anchor step
i\leq 1
trivially holds. Supposing that the claim holds for
i<j
, for some
j\geq 2
, we prove that the covariant functors
\overline{\mathbb{E}^{j}}(x,-)
and
\overline{\mathbb{E}}^{j}(x,-)
are naturally isomorphic for any choice of

and the induction hypothesis that

\overline{\mathbb{E}^{j}}(x,-)\cong\overline{\mathbb{E}^{j-1}}(x^{\prime},-)\cong\overline{\mathbb{E}}^{j-1}(x^{\prime},-)\cong\overline{\mathbb{E}}^{j}(x,-),

which establishes the inductive step and concludes the proof of
(i)
.

We prove
(ii)
under the assumptions that
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
has enough projectives, the case of enough injectives being dual. We proceed by induction. To establish the anchor step

5.2.*
5.2.*

5.2.*

Compare with Gorsky–Nakaoka–Palu

For the inductive step, suppose that the assertion holds for all
i<j
, for some

By the induction hypothesis, the vanishing of

whence the the vanishing of

. Putting it all together, the vanishing of
{\mathbb{E}}^{j}(x,y)
is equivalent to the vanishing of
\overline{\mathbb{E}}^{j}(x,y)

{\mathbb{E}}^{i}(x,y)
is equivalent to the vanishing of
\overline{\mathbb{E}}^{i}(x,y)

(ii)

5.3.
Definition

[
Oga22
, Definition 3.2]

[
NP19
, Definition 4.1]

Let
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
be an extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category. Given two additive subcategories
\mathcal{U}
and
\mathcal{V}
of
\mathcal{C}
that are closed under isomorphism and direct summands, consider the following conditions.

(CT1)

For every
u\in\mathcal{U}
and
v\in\mathcal{V}
, we have that
\mathbb{E}(u,v)=0
.

(CT3r)

For every
x\in\mathcal{C}
, there exists a conflation in
\mathcal{C}
of the form

(5.3.a)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x^{\mathcal{V}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x^{\mathcal{U}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x,}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}

in which
p
is a right
\mathcal{U}
-approximation and
x^{\mathcal{V}}\in\mathcal{V}
.

(CT3l)

For every
x\in\mathcal{C}
, there exists a conflation in
\mathcal{C}
of the form

(5.3.b)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x_{\mathcal{V}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x_{\mathcal{U}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}

in which
i
is a left
\mathcal{V}
-approximation and
x_{\mathcal{U}}\in\mathcal{U}
.

We say that the pair
(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{V})
is a
right cotorsion pair
(resp.
left cotorsion pair
) in
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
if
(CT2)
and
(CT3r)
(resp.
(CT2)
and
(CT3l)
) hold. The pair
(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{V})
is a
cotorsion pair
in
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})

(CT1)
,
(CT3r)
, and
(CT3l)
hold.

5.4.

A pair which is both a left cotorsion pair and a right cotorsion pair need not be a cotorsion pair, since we are not requiring the condition
(CT1)
to be met. For example, if the extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category
\mathcal{C}
non-semisimple (i.e.
\mathbb{E}
is a non-zero bifunctor), then
(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{C})
is a both a left and a right cotorsion pair, but not a cotorsion pair.

For a cotorsion pair
(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{V})
, it can be shown that
x\in\mathcal{U}
if and only if
\mathbb{E}(x,v)=0
for all
v\in\mathcal{V}
, and dually that
x\in\mathcal{V}
if and only if
\mathbb{E}(u,x)=0
for all
u\in\mathcal{U}

[
NP19
, Remark 4.4]
.
Moreover, both
\mathcal{U}
and
\mathcal{V}
are extension-closed in
\mathcal{C}

[
NP19
, Remark 4.6]
.

Note that
(CT2)
follows from
(CT3l)
as soon as
\mathcal{U}
is extension-closed, or dually from
(CT3r)
as soon as
\mathcal{V}
is extension-closed. Indeed, if
(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{V})
is a cotorsion pair and

5.5.

If
\mathcal{M}
is a silting subcategory of
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
, then
({{}^{\perp}\mathcal{M}},\mathcal{M}^{\perp})
is a cotorsion pair in
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
such that
{{}^{\perp}\mathcal{M}}\cap\mathcal{M}^{\perp}=\mathcal{M}

[
AT22
, Proposition 5.10]
.
Moreover, we have that
\mathcal{M}^{\vee}={{}^{\perp}\mathcal{M}}
and that
\mathcal{M}^{\wedge}=\mathcal{M}^{\perp}
.
For a rigid subcategory
\mathcal{R}
of
\mathcal{C}
, we have that
\mathcal{R}
is silting in
\thick(\mathcal{R})
, whence we deduce that
\mathcal{R}=\mathcal{R}^{\vee}\cap\mathcal{R}^{\wedge}
. Futhermore, we have that
\mathcal{R}^{\perp}=(\mathcal{R}^{\vee})^{\perp}
and
{{}^{\perp}\mathcal{R}}={{}^{\perp}(\mathcal{R}^{\wedge})}

[
AT22
, Lemma 4.4]
, from which one can derive that
\thick(\mathcal{R})\cap\mathcal{R}^{\perp}=\mathcal{R}^{\wedge}
and that
\thick(\mathcal{R})\cap{{}^{\perp}\mathcal{R}}=\mathcal{R}^{\vee}

[
AT22
, Lemma 4.11]
.
It follows that
\mathcal{R}^{\vee}\cap\mathcal{R}^{\perp}=\mathcal{R}={{}^{\perp}\mathcal{R}}\cap\mathcal{R}^{\wedge}
. One uses a long-exact sequence argument (see
Section

4.4
) to show that
\mathcal{R}^{\perp}
is closed under cones, whence
\mathcal{R}^{\wedge}\subseteq\mathcal{R}^{\perp}
, and dually
\mathcal{R}^{\vee}\subseteq{{}^{\perp}\mathcal{R}}

[
AT22
, Lemma 4.3]
.

5.6.
Definition

[
Oga22
, Definition 3.2]

Let
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
be an extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category.
An ordered tuple
\big((\mathcal{U},\mathcal{V})),(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y})\big)
is called a
generalized concentric twin cotorsion pair
(or
gCTCP
for short)
5.6.*
5.6.*

5.6.*

Ogawa uses the terminology
generalized Hovey twin cotorsion pair
, which is shortened to
gHTCP
. We have altered the terminology for the following reason: the condition
(gCTCP1)
below encodes intertwining (hence
twin
) and
(gCTCP2)
encodes the concentricity.
in
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
if the pair
(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{V})
is a left cotorsion pair in
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
, the pair
(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y})
is a right cotorsion pair in
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
, and the following hold.

(gCTCP1)

\mathcal{U}\subseteq\mathcal{X}
and
\mathcal{V}\supseteq\mathcal{Y}
,

(gCTCP2)

\mathcal{U}\cap\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{X}\cap\mathcal{Y}
.

5.7.
Condition
(gCP)

Let
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
be an extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category. Consider the following condition on a rigid subcategory
\mathcal{R}
of
\mathcal{C}
:

The ordered tuple
\big((\mathcal{R}^{\vee},\mathcal{R}^{\perp}),({{}^{\perp}\mathcal{R}},\mathcal{R}^{\wedge})\big)
is a gCTCP in
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
.
5.7.*
5.7.*

5.7.*

Since all subcategories involved are extension-closed, it follows from
Section

5.4
that
(CT2)
holds for both
(\mathcal{R}^{\vee},\mathcal{R}^{\perp})
and
({{}^{\perp}\mathcal{R}},\mathcal{R}^{\wedge})
. By
Section

5.5
, it is thus equivalent to require that
(\mathcal{R}^{\vee},\mathcal{R}^{\perp})
satisfies
(CT3l)
and that
({{}^{\perp}\mathcal{R}},\mathcal{R}^{\wedge})
satisfies
(CT3r)
. Furthermore, both pairs happen to satisfy
(CT1)
.

5.8.

Although
5.7.
Condition
(gCP)
might seem technical, it applies to many interesting situations in practice. Consider first the case where
\mathcal{C}
is a triangulated
\mathit{k}
-category.
One can reformulate Iyama–Yang’s technical assumptions for silting reduction by imposing that both
(\mathcal{R}^{\vee},\mathcal{R}^{\perp})
and
({{}^{\perp}\mathcal{R}},\mathcal{R}^{\wedge})
be cotorsion pairs in
\mathcal{C}

[
LZZZ21
, Condition
(CP)
and Remark 3.4]

[
IY18
, Proposition 3.2]
.
By
Section

5.5
, this is a special instance of
5.7.
Condition
(gCP)
.
Iyama–Yang point out that their technical assumption holds when
\mathcal{C}
is Hom-finite, the rigid subcategory
\mathcal{R}
is of the form
\add(r)
for some rigid object
r\in\mathcal{C}
, and there exists a silting object having
r
as a direct summand. A particularly interesting example is
\mathcal{C}=H_{0}\per(A)
for some connective dg
\mathit{k}
-algebra
A
, and
\mathcal{R}=\add(r)
for some rigid object
r\in H_{0}\per(A)
.
In
5.9.
Theorem

5.9
below, we prove that
5.7.
Condition
(gCP)
holds for all rigid subcategories of the two-term category
H_{0}\per_{[0,1]}(A)
.

5.9.
Theorem

\mathit{k}

5.12.
Lemma

Let
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
be an extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category with enough projectives or injectives. For a rigid subcategory
\mathcal{R}\subseteq\mathcal{C}
satisfying
5.7.
Condition
(gCP)
, we have that
\mathrm{silt}_{\mathcal{R}}(\mathcal{Z}_{\mathcal{R}})=\mathrm{silt}_{\mathcal{R}}(\mathcal{C})
. In particular, the assertion in
5.2.
Proposition

5.2
(iv)
holds.

Proof.

We refer to Liu–Zhou–Zhou–Zhu
[
LZZZ21
, Lemma 3.11]
. Although their condition
(CP)
is stronger than our
5.7.
Condition
(gCP)
, the reader may check that
5.7.
Condition
(gCP)
is sufficient to conduct this proof.
5.12.*
5.12.*

5.12.*

For the special case where
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
is 0-Auslander and admits Bongartz completions, one can alternatively proceed as follows: It was asserted in
Section

4.10
that a rigid subcategory of
\mathcal{C}
is silting precisely when it is maximal with respect to the rigidity property. By
5.10.
Proposition

5.10
(iv)
, the same can be said of rigid subcategories of
\mathcal{Z}_{\mathcal{R}}
. Recalling that
\mathrm{rigid}_{\mathcal{R}}(\mathcal{Z}_{\mathcal{R}})=\mathrm{rigid}_{\mathcal{R}}(\mathcal{C})
, we now conclude, since a rigid subcategory of
\mathcal{C}
is maximal if and only if it is maximal as a rigid subcategory of
\mathcal{Z}_{\mathcal{R}}
.

∎

up to natural isomorphism, where
F
is an extriangulated functor.
The result essentially follows from a work of Ogawa
[
Oga22
, Theorem 3.10]
. Below, we spell out Ogawa’s approach, in order to convince the reader that all necessary assumptions of are met for the situation at hand.

We have assumed that
\big((\mathcal{R}^{\vee},\mathcal{R}^{\perp}),({{}^{\perp}\mathcal{R}},\mathcal{R}^{\wedge})\big)
is a gCTCP in
(\mathcal{C},\mathbb{E})
.
The left cotorsion pair

F

5.14.
Example

Let
\Lambda
be a finite-dimensional
\mathit{k}
-algebra and let
r
be a rigid object in the two-term category
\mathcal{C}=H_{0}\twoper(\Lambda)
. Then
\mathcal{C}/\thick(\mathcal{R})\simeq\overline{\mathcal{C}}_{\add(r)}\simeq H_{0}\twoper(C_{r})
, where
C_{r}
is a connective dg
\mathit{k}
-algebra
[
Gar24
]
.
The finite-dimensional
\mathit{k}
-algebra
H_{0}C_{r}
is the
\tau
-tilting reduction of
\Lambda
with respect to
r
, in the sense of Jasso
[
Jas15
]
.

5.15.*
5.15.*

5.15.*

The reader may check that the following is a counter-example: take
\mathcal{C}
to be the two-term category of the preprojective algebra of type
A_{2}
, and
\mathcal{R}
the additive closure of an indecomposable projective object.

However, every morphism in
\mathcal{C}/\thick(\mathcal{R})
takes the form
L_{\mathcal{R}}(s)^{-1}L_{\mathcal{R}}(f)L_{\mathcal{R}}(t)^{-1}
, where
s,t\in\mathcal{S}_{\thick(\mathcal{R})}

[
Oga22
, Corollary 3.11]
, where
\mathcal{S}_{\thick(\mathcal{R})}
is as defined in
Section

3.3
. Since the expression
L_{\mathcal{R}}(s)^{-1}L_{\mathcal{R}}(f)L_{\mathcal{R}}(t)^{-1}
can be thought of as the gluing of a left fraction and a right fraction, this is reasonably close to a calculus of fractions.

Corollary

(i)
and
(i)
above. We now use

6.
Picture categories and picture groups

6.1.
Definition

Let
\mathscr{A}
be a 0-Auslander exact dg
\mathit{k}
-category with
\mathit{k}
-cofibrant mapping complexes. Assume also that all rigid subcategories of
H_{0}\mathscr{A}
admit Bongartz completions. If these assumption hold, we say that the
picture category
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})
of
\mathscr{A}
is defined
.
The
picture category
of
\mathscr{A}
is denoted
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})
, and is defined in the paragraph below. By
5.16.
Corollary

5.16
(iii)
and
5.10.
Proposition

5.10
(v)
, the assumptions we have made on
\mathscr{A}
also hold for dg quotient
\mathscr{A}/\mathscr{R}
where
\mathscr{R}
is a rigid dg subcategory of
\mathscr{A}
.

and

satisfies the following:

(i)

the subcategory
\varpi^{-1}_{\mathscr{R}_{1}}(\mathscr{R}_{2})
of
\mathscr{L}_{1}
is rigid,

(ii)

the dg quotient
(\mathscr{L}_{1}/\mathscr{R}_{1})/\mathscr{R}_{2}
is naturally identified with
\mathscr{L}_{1}/\varpi_{\mathscr{R}_{1}}^{-1}(\mathscr{R}_{2})
.

The first assertion follows directly from
5.16.
Corollary

5.16
(iv)
. The second is deduced from
5.16.
Corollary

5.16
(v)
; the dg
\mathit{k}
-category
\mathscr{L}_{1}/\mathscr{R}_{1}
has
\mathit{k}
-cofibrant mapping complexes, so the morphisms
\varpi_{\varpi_{\mathscr{R}_{1}}^{-1}(\mathscr{R}_{2})}
and
\varpi_{\mathscr{R}_{2}}\circ\varpi_{\mathscr{R}_{1}}
coincide in
\bf 0\mathchar 45\relax\!Aus_{\mathit{k}}
, which amounts to that
(\mathscr{L}_{1}/\mathscr{R}_{1})/\mathscr{R}_{2}\simeq\mathscr{L}_{1}/(\varpi_{\mathscr{R}_{1}}^{-1}(\mathscr{R}_{2}))
in
\bf 0\mathchar 45\relax\!Aus_{\mathit{k}}
.

6.3.
Proposition

Let
\mathscr{A}
be a 0-Auslander exact dg
\mathit{k}
-category for which the picture category
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})
of
\mathscr{A}
is defined.
Then
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})
is a category.
6.3.*
6.3.*

6.3.*

The proof below closely resembles that of the special case of connective dg
\mathit{k}
-algebras with finite-dimensional homology in all degrees, as was established in previous work
[
Bør21
, Theorem 4.3]

Proof.

It is clear from the construction that the identity morphism at an object
\mathscr{L}\in\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})
is provided by the rigid dg subcategory of
\mathscr{L}
consisting of the zero objects. It remains to show that the composition rule defined above is associative. Given three composable morphisms

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}_{3}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}_{4},}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{R}_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{R}_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{R}_{3}}

it is to be shown that

(6.3.a)

\varpi^{-1}_{\varpi_{\mathscr{R}_{1}}^{-1}(\mathscr{R}_{2})}(\mathscr{R}_{3})=\varpi^{-1}_{\mathscr{R}_{1}}\big(\varpi_{\mathscr{R}_{2}}^{-1}(\mathscr{R}_{3})\big),

as rigid dg subcategories of
\mathscr{A}
. Since
\varpi_{\mathscr{R}_{1}}^{-1}(\mathscr{R}_{2})
is a rigid dg subcategory of
\mathscr{A}
containing
\mathscr{R}_{1}
,
5.16.
Corollary

5.16
(v)
enables the decomposition of the localization morphism
\varpi_{\varpi_{\mathscr{R}_{1}}^{-1}(\mathscr{R}_{2})}
as
\varpi_{\mathscr{R}_{2}}\circ\varpi_{\mathscr{R}_{1}}
. As a result, we have that
\varpi_{\varpi_{\mathscr{R}_{1}}^{-1}(\mathscr{R}_{2})}
and
\varpi_{\mathscr{R}_{2}}\circ\varpi_{\mathscr{R}_{1}}
induce the same bijection from
\mathrm{rigid}_{\varpi_{\mathscr{R}_{1}}^{-1}(\mathscr{R}_{2})}(\mathscr{L}_{1})
to
\mathrm{rigid}(\mathscr{L}_{3})
.
The application of the inverses of these coincident bijections to
\mathscr{R}_{3}
gives the equality in (
6.3.a
), whence the proof is complete.
∎

6.4.
Definition

Let
\mathscr{A}
be a 0-Auslander exact dg
\mathit{k}
-category for which the picture category
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})
of
\mathscr{A}
is defined.

(i)

The
picture space
of
\mathscr{A}
is denoted
\mathfrak{X}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathscr{A}}}\right)
, and defined as the classifying space
\mathrm{B}\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})
.

(ii)

The
picture group
of
\mathscr{A}
is denoted
{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathscr{A}}}\right)
, and defined as the fundamental group
\pi_{1}(\mathfrak{X}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathscr{A}}}\right),\mathscr{O})
, where
\mathscr{O}
is a trivial dg
\mathit{k}
-category.

6.5.
Example

A
be a dg
k
-algebra with finite-dimensional homology in all degrees and let
\mathscr{A}=\twoper(A)
be the two-term dg
\mathit{k}
-category of

(see
4.6.
Example

4.6
(i)
). Then the category
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})
is equivalent to the
\tau
-cluster morphism category of
A
, as defined in previous work
[
Bør21
]
. This can be shown directly by spelling out the definition provided in the cited reference.

\mathfrak{W}(A)

, and so on.

, whence one can restrict to the special case of finite-dimensional
\mathit{k}
-algebras without loss of generality, up to equivalence of categories.
For finite-dimensional
\mathit{k}
-algebras, there are several instances of worked examples in the literature
[
BM21
, §12]

[
BH23
, §7]
. A particularly easy example is that of a local
\mathit{k}
-algebra
\Lambda
, whose picture category can be displayed as

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\twoper(\Lambda)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{O},}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Lambda}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sigma\Lambda}

where the arrows are labeled by the rigid object generating the rigid dg subcategory of
\twoper(\Lambda)
in question. The picture space of
\Lambda
is a circle, and the picture group becomes free abelian with one generator.

We include a small example to illustrate what can happen in the non-reduced case. The 0-Auslander extriangulated
\mathit{k}
-category
\mathrm{mod}(\Lambda_{2})
in
4.6.
Example

4.6
(ii)
is Quillen exact and contains a projective generator, whence it admits an exact dg enhancement
\mathscr{A}
whose picture category is defined. The
\mathit{k}
-category
\mathrm{mod}(\Lambda_{2})
contains three objects up to isomorphism, namely
n
,
p
, and
i
, where
n
is projective-injective, the object
p
is projective and non-injective, and
i
is injective and non-projective.
Every indecomposable object in
\mathrm{mod}(\Lambda_{2})
is rigid, and will be tacitly identified with the rigid dg subcategory of
\mathscr{A}
it generates. We thus write
\mathscr{A}/x
for the dg quotient of
\mathscr{A}
modulo the smallest additive dg subcategory of
\mathscr{A}
containing
x
.
The picture category
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})
can then be displayed as follows:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}/p}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}/n}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}/i}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{O}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varpi_{p}(p\oplus n)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptscriptstyle\varpi_{n}(p\oplus n)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptscriptstyle\varpi_{n}(i\oplus n)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varpi_{i}(i\oplus n)}

where the two shaded squares are commutative. There are two morphisms from
\mathscr{A}
to
\mathscr{O}
, namely
p\oplus n
and
i\oplus n
.
Note that
\mathscr{A}/n
is quasi-equivalent to
\twoper(\mathit{k})
, and that the full subcategory of
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})
spanned by
\mathscr{A}/n
and

is equivalent to
\mathfrak{W}(\mathit{k})
. It is moreover easy to see that the picture space
\mathfrak{X}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathscr{A}}}\right)
to homotopy equivalent to
\mathfrak{X}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathit{k}}}\right)
, an assertion we generalize in
6.6.
Proposition

6.6

6.6.
Proposition

Let
\mathscr{A}
be a 0-Auslander exact dg
\mathit{k}
-category for which the picture category
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})
of
\mathscr{A}
is defined, and let
\mathscr{N}
denote the rigid dg subcategory of
\mathscr{A}
consisting of all projective-injective objects in
\mathscr{A}
. The space
\mathfrak{X}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathscr{A}/\mathscr{N}}}\right)
is then a deformation retract of
\mathfrak{X}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathscr{A}}}\right)
.
In particular, the inclusion functor
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A}/\mathscr{N})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})}
induces a homotopy equivalence
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{X}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathscr{A}/\mathscr{N}}}\right)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{X}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathscr{A}}}\right)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sim}
and thus an isomorphism of picture groups
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathscr{A}/\mathscr{N}}}\right)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathscr{A}}}\right).}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sim}

One consequently recovers all possible homotopy types of picture spaces, as well as all isomorphism classes of picture groups, by only considering reduced 0-Auslander exact dg
\mathit{k}
-categories.
More generally, if
\mathscr{R}
is a rigid dg subcategory of
\mathscr{A}
in which all objects are projective-injective, the inclusion functor
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A}/\mathscr{R})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})}
induces a homotopy equivalence of picture spaces
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{X}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathscr{A}/\mathscr{R}}}\right)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{X}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathscr{A}}}\right)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sim}
and thus an isomorphism of picture groups
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathscr{A}/\mathscr{R}}}\right)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathscr{A}}}\right).}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sim}

Proof.

Since
\mathscr{R}
is a full dg subcategory of
\mathscr{N}
, we have consecutive inclusions

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{X}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathscr{A}/\mathscr{N}}}\right)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{X}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathscr{A}/\mathscr{R}}}\right)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{X}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathscr{A}}}\right).}

One uses the two-out-of-three property for homotopy equivalences to deduce our claim concerning
\mathscr{R}
from our claim concerning
\mathscr{N}
. To complete the proof, we show that the inclusion functor
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A}/\mathscr{N})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})}
admits a left adjoint
[
Qui73
, Corollary 1 in §1]
.

as desired.
∎

6.7.

Henceforth in this section, we describe the structure of picture categories and picture groups. Note first that
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})
is a skeletal category by definition, in the sense that isomorphic objects in
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})
are equal.
The object
\mathscr{A}
in
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})
is
weakly initial
, i.e. there exists a morphism from
\mathscr{A}
to any other object in
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})
by definition. The trivial dg
\mathit{k}
-category
\mathscr{O}
is a weakly terminal object in
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})
, since it occurs as a dg quotient of any
\mathscr{L}\in\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})
modulo a silting subcategory of
\mathscr{L}
. The existence of a weakly initial (or weakly terminal) object in
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})
makes picture space
\mathfrak{X}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathscr{A}}}\right)
a connected topological space.
The morphism set
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})(\mathscr{A},\mathscr{O})
is precisely the set of silting subcategories of
\mathscr{A}
. More generally, the morphism set
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})(\mathscr{L},\mathscr{O})
is precisely the set of silting subcategories of
\mathscr{L}
. Unless
\mathscr{L}
is equal to
\mathscr{A}
(resp.
\mathscr{O}
), the morphism set
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})(\mathscr{L},\mathscr{A})
(resp.
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})(\mathscr{O},\mathscr{L})
) will be empty.
For a rigid dg subcategory
\mathscr{R}
of
\mathscr{A}
, the picture category
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A}/\mathscr{R})
embeds into
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})
.

6.8.

Let
\mathscr{A}
be a 0-Auslander dg
\mathit{k}
-category for which the picture category
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})
of
\mathscr{A}
is defined. Suppose that
H_{0}\mathscr{A}
is Krull–Schmidt and contains a silting object
t
with
n
non-isomorphic indecomposable direct summands. By combining the assertions in the paragraphs below, we will show that
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})
is a
cubical category
, in the sense of Igusa
[
Igu14
, Definition 3.2]
, whereby generalizing a result of Hanson–Igusa, who show that the picture category of a finite-dimensional
\mathit{k}
-algebra is cubical
[
HI21b
, Theorem 2.14]
.

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}\hskip 0.86108pt}{}\mathscr{L}_{2}
, then
\mathscr{R}^{\prime}
must be given by a direct summand of
r
. Let
\mathrm{faq}(\mathscr{R})
denote the subcategory of
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})
consisting of the morphisms
\mathscr{Q}
such that
\mathscr{R}=\mathscr{Q}_{2}\circ\mathscr{Q}\circ\mathscr{Q}_{1}
for some morphisms
\mathscr{Q}_{1}
and
\mathscr{Q}_{2}
. One shows that
\mathrm{faq}(\mathscr{R})
is the image of a faithful embedding into
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})
of a Boolean lattice of rank
\ell
(there is one object in
\mathrm{faq}(\mathscr{R})
for every direct summand of
r
). This is to say that
\mathrm{faq}(\mathscr{R})
takes the form of an
\ell
-dimensional hypercube.

We keep the notation introduced in the last paragraph.
The set
\{\mathscr{R}_{i}\}
of rigid dg subcategories of

6.9.

Although we have defined picture groups as the fundamental group of the picture space, we will in practice treat it as the fundamental group of the picture category. We slightly adapt the setup of Evrard
[
Evr73
,
Evr75
]

[
Qui73
, §1]
. A
loop
in
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})
with basepoint
\mathscr{O}
is either the trivial path on
\mathscr{O}
or a zig-zag
\gamma
of morphisms in
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})
of the form

(6.9.a)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{O}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}_{m}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathscr{L}_{m-1,m}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathscr{L}_{1,2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{O}}

The
length
of the loop above is
m
, whereas the trivial loop has length 0. In (
6.9.a
), the object
\mathscr{L}_{i}
is the
i^{\mathit{th}}
term
of
\gamma
.

Let
\gamma_{1}
and
\gamma_{2}
be loops on
\mathscr{O}
, of length
m
and
p
, respectively.
The
concatenation
of
\gamma_{1}
and
\gamma_{2}
is denoted by
\gamma_{2}\gamma_{1}
and defined by

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{O}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{O}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}_{p}^{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}_{1}^{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}_{m}^{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}_{1}^{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{O}}
\underbrace{\hskip 175.00026pt}_{\gamma_{2}}
\underbrace{\hskip 175.00026pt}_{\gamma_{1}}

An
elementary homotopy
from
\gamma_{1}
to
\gamma_{2}
is given by a strictly increasing function
f\colon[1,m]\cap\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow[1,p]\cap\mathbb{Z}
and a commutative diagram

(6.9.b)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f(\gamma_{1})\colon}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{O}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}_{m}^{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathscr{L}_{1,2}^{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}_{1}^{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}_{1}^{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{O}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\gamma_{2}\colon}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{O}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}_{p}^{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}_{f(1),f(1)+1}^{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}_{f(1)}^{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}_{1}^{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{O}}

where the bottom row displays
\gamma_{2}
and the top row the
elongation
of
\gamma_{1}
along
f
(there are
f_{i+1}-f_{i}
copies of
\mathscr{L}_{i}
in the top row, where
f_{i}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{\mbox{\scriptsize{def}}}}}{{\,=\,}}f(i)
for
i\geq 1
and
f_{0}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{\mbox{\scriptsize{def}}}}}{{\,=\,}}0
).
The notion of elementary homotopy determines a binary relation on the set of loops, whose symmetric and transitive closure provides a suitable notion of homotopy. Explicitly, two loops are said to be
homotopic
if there exists a zig-zag of elementary homotopies from one to the other.

With the definitions above, one defines the fundamental group of
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})
as the set homotopy classes of loops on
\mathscr{O}
equipped with the binary operation of concatenation. This is group is clearly isomorphic to the picture group of
\mathscr{A}
, as defined in
6.4.
Definition

(ii)
.

6.10.

Recall that an
interval
in a poset
({P},\leq)
is a subposet of
{P}
of the form

[a,b]\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{\mbox{\scriptsize{def}}}}}{{\,=\,}}\{x\in{P}\,\,|\,\,a\leq x\leq b\},

where
a,b\in{P}
. Let
\mathrm{int}({P})
denote the set of intervals in
{P}
. An interval
[a,b]
is said to be
irreducible
if its cardinality is exactly
2
.

Our next result should be compared with presentations of picture groups that have been established for the special case of
\mathbf{g}
-finite finite-dimensional algebras over fields
[
HI21b
, Proposition 4.4]
.

(ii)

The kernel of the homomorphism (
6.11.b
) is generated by expressions of the form

{[\mathscr{S}_{1},\mathscr{S}_{2}]}^{-1}{[\mathscr{S}_{1},\mathscr{S}_{1.5}]}{[\mathscr{S}_{1.5},\mathscr{S}_{2}]},

where
[\mathscr{S}_{1},\mathscr{S}_{1.5}]
and
[\mathscr{S}_{1.5},\mathscr{S}_{2}]
are consecutive intervals in
\mathrm{silt}(\mathscr{A})
. In particular, if
\mathscr{A}
is
\mathbf{g}
-finite, the picture group
{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathscr{A}}}\right)
is finitely presented, and generated by the irreducible intervals in
\mathrm{silt}(\mathscr{A})
.

{{}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{}{{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
}{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{-1.73619pt}{6.75519pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform=matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -2.4 9.35)} \pgfsys@hbox{58}\lxSVG@closescope }}}

{{}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{}{{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
}{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{2.63889pt}{-1.81079pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform=matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 3.65 -2.51)} \pgfsys@hbox{58}\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}\hskip 0.86108pt}\mathscr{O}
in
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})
. One sets up a homotopy

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{O}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}_{m}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathscr{L}_{1,2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{O}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{O}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}_{m}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathscr{L}_{1,2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{O}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{O}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}_{m}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{L}_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{O}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{O}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{Q}_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{Q}_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{R}_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{S}_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{Q}_{2}\circ\mathscr{R}_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{R}_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{S}_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{S}_{2}}

where
\mathscr{S}_{1}=\mathscr{Q}_{1}\circ\mathscr{R}_{1}
and
\mathscr{S}_{2}=\mathscr{R}_{2}\circ\mathscr{Q}_{2}\circ\mathscr{R}_{1}
. The bottom row is now a composite of loops of length shorter than
m
. By the induction hypothesis, we can express the bottom row as a concatenation of loops in the image of
\gamma_{(-)}
, or inverses of such, whereby we conclude the proof of
(i)
.

We move on to
(ii)
. It is clear that the kernel of the homomorphism
\gamma
is generated by expressions of the form
\gamma_{2}^{-1}\gamma_{1}
, where
\gamma_{1}
and
\gamma_{2}
are related by elementary homotopy. Using
(i)
, we can further assume said elementary homotopy to be of the following form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{O}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{O}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{O}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{O}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{O}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{O}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{O}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{S}_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{S}_{1.5}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{S}_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{S}_{1.5}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{S}_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{S}_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{S}_{1.5}}
\underbrace{\hskip 200.0003pt}_{D}

where either
\mathscr{S}_{1}\leq\mathscr{S}_{1.5}\leq\mathscr{S}_{2}
or
\mathscr{S}_{2}\leq\mathscr{S}_{1.5}\leq\mathscr{S}_{1}
. The whole diagram can be built from subdiagrams of the same form as
D
, and
D
is itself an elementary homotopy of loops. Since
D
encodes a relation of the appropriate form, or the inverse of such an expression, we can conclude that
(ii)
holds.

We now prove
(iii)
. Having shown in
(ii)
that
\gamma
sends the irreducible intervals in
\mathrm{silt}(\mathscr{A})
to a set of generators, it suffices to show that every such generator is homotopic to a loop of the form
\overline{\gamma}_{B}
, where
B\in\mathfrak{B}(\mathscr{A})
. Given an irreducible interval
[\mathscr{S}_{1},\mathscr{S}_{2}]
in
\mathrm{silt}(\mathscr{A})
, let
s_{1}
and
s_{2}
be the silting objects in
H_{0}\mathscr{A}
determining
\mathscr{S}_{1}
and
\mathscr{S}_{2}
, respectively, and let
r
be the rigid object such that
H_{0}(\mathscr{S}_{1}\cap\mathscr{S}_{2})=\add(r)
(see
Section

4.10
).
Consider the following diagram in
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})
:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}/(\mathscr{S}_{1}\cap\mathscr{S}_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{O}.}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{S}_{1}\cap\mathscr{S}_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varpi_{\mathscr{S}_{1}\cap\mathscr{S}_{2}}(\mathscr{S}_{1})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varpi_{\mathscr{S}_{1}\cap\mathscr{S}_{2}}(\mathscr{S}_{2})}

The two composites are the silting subcategories
\mathscr{S}_{1}
and
\mathscr{S}_{2}
. Since
s_{1}
and
s_{2}
are the only rigid objects in
H_{0}\mathscr{A}
properly containing
r
as a direct summand, the morphisms
\varpi_{\mathscr{S}_{1}\cap\mathscr{S}_{2}}(\mathscr{S}_{1})
and
\varpi_{\mathscr{S}_{1}\cap\mathscr{S}_{2}}(\mathscr{S}_{2})
are the only ones in
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})
with domain
\mathscr{A}/(\mathscr{S}_{1}\cap\mathscr{S}_{2})
. Consequently, we have that
\mathscr{A}/(\mathscr{S}_{1}\cap\mathscr{S}_{2})\in\mathfrak{B}(\mathscr{A})
.
The construction of the (elementary) homotopy

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{O}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{O}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{O}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}/(\mathscr{S}_{1}\cap\mathscr{S}_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{O}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{S}_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{S}_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{S}_{1}\cap\mathscr{S}_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varpi_{\mathscr{S}_{1}\cap\mathscr{S}_{2}}(\mathscr{S}_{2})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varpi_{\mathscr{S}_{1}\cap\mathscr{S}_{2}}(\mathscr{S}_{1})}

concludes the proof.
∎

is defined,

7.2.

The existence of faithful group functors, along with the cubical structure of picture categories (see
Section

6.8
), can be useful to determine the homotopy type of picture spaces. Indeed, a cubical category
\mathcal{C}
is locally
\mathrm{CAT}(0)
precisely when the conditions
(I1)
–
(I3)
below are met
[
Igu14
, Propositions 3.4 and 3.7]
. In particular, these conditions ensure that the classifying space
\mathrm{B}\mathcal{C}
is an Eilenberg–MacLane space of type
\K(\pi,1)

[
Gro87
]
, which is to say that the homotopy groups
\pi_{i}(\mathrm{B}\mathcal{C},\ast)
are trivial for all
i\geq 2
.

(I1)

Since the picture space
\mathfrak{X}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathscr{A}}}\right)
is connected, as was argued in

6.7
, we can thus determine its homotopy type if the conditions
(I1)
–
(I3)
above are met.

7.3.

It is straightforward to show that the condition
(I1)
above holds for the picture category
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})
of a 0-Auslander exact dg
\mathit{k}
-category
\mathscr{A}
with a silting object. Less trivially, we will prove that
(I3)
holds for
\mathfrak{W}(\mathscr{A})
when
\mathit{k}
is the field of complex numbers
[
Bø
]
. This will be achieved with the aid of motivic Hall algebras.

[
Bri17

when defining the completed motivic Hall algebra
\widehat{\mathrm{H}}(\mathscr{A})

\mathscr{A}

\widehat{G}_{\mathrm{Hall}}(\mathscr{A})
corresponding to the pro-nilpotent Lie
\mathbb{Q}(t)

\widehat{\mathrm{H}}(\mathscr{A})
